summary:
Same-sex relations are criminalised in Eswatini for men and women throughout the country, as recorded on 12 March 2026. No legal gender recognition is available, so a trans visitor's passport and other documents are read exactly as issued, with no route to align them with lived gender.

LGBTI organisations cannot obtain official registration. Eswatini's registrar of companies refused to register a sexual and gender minorities group in June 2019 on grounds of morality, and in April 2022 the High Court upheld that refusal while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. A visitor should not expect to find a registered national advocacy body to contact for assistance.

Hostility from official figures is documented. A 2021 United States State Department report found that some traditional, religious and government officials publicly criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In June 2012 the prime minister stated that people of the same sex could not even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not ready to consider the question, and in 2014 a government press secretary said the government was monitoring the situation in order to take a legal position.

Public visibility has nonetheless been tolerated on several occasions. The first Eswatini Pride, held in July 2018, was reported as a great success, a virtual Pride celebration held in June 2021 passed without incident, and a church welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in December 2018 at a time when discrimination in the kingdom showed no let-up.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex relationships. Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced.

Healthcare carries a documented outing and refusal risk. A 2019 survey found that 59% of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities and 30% had been denied healthcare services.

Anti-LGBT violence has produced fatalities. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who said he did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. Rock of Hope states that, with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and that most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa.

No broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity exist in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. A 2012 statement by the then foreign affairs minister rejected a United Nations working group call for an LGBTQ protection law on the grounds that so few gay people lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House rated Eswatini Not Free in Freedom in the World 2024, with an overall score of 17 out of 100, comprising 1 out of 40 for political rights and 16 out of 60 for civil liberties, describing an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space.

The closure of LGBTI organisational space sits inside a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment. The BTI 2024 country report records that the government denies LGBTQ+ groups the ability to register as organisations within an oppressive environment in which 'Mswati must fall' has become a common protest slogan.

Media regulation carries a counterweight. The 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation.

Self-reported harm among LGBTQ Swazis is high. A 2013 survey found that 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances in order to feel normal.

External pressure has been persistent but ineffective. In May 2017 the United Nations Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
localsOnly:
Residents have several policy instruments that name sexual orientation or gender identity without creating enforceable rights. Section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion.

The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of one's sex or sexual orientation, define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity, and name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence.

The National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles, and the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation.

Public health outreach has at times included men who have sex with men. In February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, and the deputy director of health, Simon Zwane, said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples, a move LGBTQ groups welcomed.

In May 2017 the United Nations Human Rights Committee pressed the government on protection measures, and in 2012 the then foreign affairs minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a United Nations working group call for an LGBTQ protection law as not worth the effort given the small number of gay people in Eswatini.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents prosecutions or arrests under the sodomy provisions, so the frequency and manner of enforcement of the criminal law against same-sex relations remains unresolved.

No source addresses entry, visa or border screening of transgender travellers, including whether documents are inspected against presentation or whether any screening question risks disclosure. This is not sourced either way.

The absence of legal gender recognition is stated at the level of overall possibility; no source specifies which Eswatini-issued documents carry a gender marker, whether any amendment procedure exists for a passport, or how consular or airline systems treat a mismatch between presentation and document.

The claims on relationship non-recognition, adoption prohibition and the April 2022 High Court ruling are drawn from a Wikipedia country page rather than from the text of the relevant statute or the judgment itself; the underlying legislation and the judgment have not been verified directly here.

The April 2022 High Court acceptance that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression did not overturn the refusal to register the group, and the practical effect of that constitutional finding on future registration attempts is unresolved.

The most recent consolidated source is dated 12 March 2026; no reporting after that date is available in the inventory, so any change since then is not sourced.
